title: Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
section: A cricket decision before the theory
text:
A cricket decision before the theory
A cricket team is defending 12 runs in the final over.
The captain must choose one of three bowlers:

a fast bowler;
a spinner;
a medium-pace bowler.

The batting side may respond aggressively or may focus on rotating the strike.

Think for one minute
Question: Which bowler should the captain choose?
Do not calculate anything yet.
What information would you want before making the decision?


Class discussion
Possible answers include:

How has each bowler performed against aggressive batting?
How has each bowler performed when batters rotate the strike?
What is the pitch like?
Is one bowler more likely to concede boundaries?
Is one bowler better at limiting singles?
What is the estimated chance of successfully defending the target?

The key point is simple:

A decision is made now, but its consequence often depends on something that happens later and is not fully under our control.

That is the setting in which decision theory becomes useful.

title: Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
text:
3.1 Decision alternatives
A decision alternative is an action available to the decision maker.
The decision maker can choose among the alternatives.

Cricket example
Suppose a captain must choose a bowler for the final over.

(A_1): Fast bowler
(A_2): Spin bowler
(A_3): Medium-pace bowler

These are decision alternatives because the captain controls the choice.


Quick question
Which of the following is a decision alternative?

The batter attacks
The pitch offers turn
The captain selects the spinner
The batting side scores 10 runs

Answer: 3. The captain selects the spinner.

title: Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
text:
3.2 States of nature
A state of nature is a possible future condition that affects the consequence of a decision but is not controlled by the decision maker.

Cricket example
Suppose the captain chooses the final-over bowler.
Possible states of nature could be:

(S_1): The batter attacks aggressively
(S_2): The batter focuses on strike rotation

The captain chooses the bowler.
The captain does not control how the batter responds.
So:

Bowler choice = decision alternative
Batter response = state of nature



Athletics example
A 1500 m runner must decide on a pacing strategy.
Possible alternatives:

(A_1): Fast early pace
(A_2): Even pace
(A_3): Conservative start with fast finish

Possible states of nature:

(S_1): Competitors make the race fast
(S_2): Competitors make the race tactical and slow

The athlete controls the race plan but does not control the pace chosen by the rest of the field.


Volleyball example
A volleyball team is receiving serve at 23–23.
The coach may choose:

(A_1): Middle attack
(A_2): Outside attack
(A_3): Back-row attack

Possible states of nature:

(S_1): Opponent commits the middle block
(S_2): Opponent forms a strong outside double block
(S_3): Opponent uses a balanced block

The attacking team controls its own choice.
The opponent’s defensive response is not under its control.

Identify the components

Decision alternatives

(A_1): Fast bowler
(A_2): Spin bowler
(A_3): Medium pace



States of nature

(S_1): Batter attacks
(S_2): Batter rotates strike



Consequence
Expected runs conceded.
Here, smaller values are preferred.
So the table behaves like a loss table.

title: Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
text:
How to read the table
If the captain chooses the spinner and the batter attacks, then:
[ C_{21}=8 ]
Interpretation:

If the captain chooses the spinner and the batter attacks, the expected number of runs conceded is 8.

Similarly:
[ C_{12}=7 ]
Interpretation:

If the captain chooses the fast bowler and the batter rotates the strike, the expected number of runs conceded is 7.


Stop and interpret

Which bowler performs best if the batter attacks?
Which bowler performs best if the batter rotates the strike?
Which bowler has the largest possible expected runs conceded?
Can we choose the overall best bowler from this table alone?

Answers

Spin bowler, with 8 expected runs conceded.
Fast bowler, with 7 expected runs conceded.
Fast bowler, with 12 expected runs conceded.
Not yet. We still need a rule for comparing alternatives when the future batting response is unknown.

title: Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory

Cricket as a payoff problem
Suppose the analyst instead estimates the probability of successfully defending the target.



Bowling decision
Batter attacks
Batter rotates strike




Fast bowler
0.43
0.71


Spin bowler
0.64
0.56


Medium pace

Now larger values are preferred.
This is a payoff table.

The underlying decision problem may be similar, but the direction of preference changes with the consequence measure.

Runs conceded: lower is better.
Probability of winning: higher is better.

Now larger values are preferred.
This immediately shows an important feature of decision problems:

The action that looks best depends on the state of nature.

There is no single strategy that dominates in both race conditions.

title: Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
text:
Template
For any sports decision problem, identify:

Decision maker
Who chooses the action?


Alternatives
What can be chosen?
Use notation such as (A_1, A_2, , A_m).


States of nature
What uncertain future conditions may occur?
Use notation such as (S_1, S_2, , S_n).


Consequences
What happens if (A_i) is selected and (S_j) occurs?
Use (C_{ij}) for the corresponding consequence.


Available information
What is currently known about the states of nature?

title: Week 01: Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
text:
8-minute activity: Volleyball serving decision
A volleyball coach must decide whether to keep the current server or introduce a serving specialist late in the set.
Two possible reception states are considered:

the opponent receives well;
the opponent receives poorly.

The estimated probability of winning the rally is:



Decision
Good opponent reception
Poor opponent reception




Keep current server
0.43
0.62


Use serving specialist
0.35
0.76




Work in pairs

Identify the decision maker.
Identify the decision alternatives.
Identify the states of nature.
Identify the consequence.
Find (C_{12}).
Find (C_{21}).
Which action would be selected if good reception were known with certainty?
Which action would be selected if poor reception were known with certainty?
Can one action be selected for the next serve without using an additional decision criterion? Explain briefly.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Situation A: Certainty
The captain knows that the next batter will play aggressively throughout the over.
There is only one relevant state for the decision.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Situation B: Uncertainty
The captain knows that the batter may either:

attack aggressively; or
focus on rotating the strike.

However, there is no reliable information about which response is more likely.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Situation C: Risk
The captain has historical information suggesting:

(P() = 0.65)
(P() = 0.35)

These are three different decision-making environments.

Opening question
What changes across the three situations?
Not the alternatives.
The captain still chooses between pace and spin.
What changes is the information about the state of nature.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Definition
A decision is made under certainty when the relevant future state is known.
The decision maker can directly compare the consequences of the available actions under that known state.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Athletics example
A 400 m athlete is choosing between two warm-up routines before an indoor race.
The environmental conditions are already known and fixed.
Suppose the estimated race times are:



Warm-up routine
Expected 400 m time




Routine A
51.8 s


Routine B
52.4 s



Since lower race time is preferred,
[ 51.8 < 52.4 ]
so Routine A is preferred.

Under certainty, we do not need probabilities for several future states because the relevant state is treated as known.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Cricket example
Suppose the captain knows the next batter is especially weak against spin.
Estimated runs conceded are:



Bowling decision
Known batter condition




Fast bowler
9


Spin bowler
6



Since fewer runs conceded are preferred, spin is the better action under the known condition.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Definition
A decision is made under uncertainty when:

more than one state of nature is possible;
the decision maker does not know which state will occur; and
reliable probabilities cannot be assigned to the states.

The important point is that the possible states can still be described.
What is missing is their probability distribution.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Volleyball example
A volleyball coach must choose an attacking strategy at a critical point.
The alternatives are:

(A_1): middle attack
(A_2): outside attack
(A_3): back-row attack

Possible defensive states are:

(S_1): opponent commits the middle block
(S_2): opponent forms an outside double block
(S_3): opponent uses a balanced block

Suppose the estimated probability of winning the rally under each combination is:



Attack
Middle block
Outside double block
Balanced block




Middle attack
0.34
0.63
0.48


Outside attack
0.60
0.31
0.46


Back-row attack
0.50
0.56
0.43



The coach knows the possible defensive responses.
But suppose there is no reliable probability model for which blocking pattern will be used.
This is decision making under uncertainty.

Class question
Can we calculate an expected value for each attack?
No.
To calculate an expected value, we need probabilities for the states of nature.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Athletics example
A 1500 m runner is preparing for a championship final.
Possible race strategies are:

fast early pace;
even pace;
conservative start with a fast finish.

Possible race states are:

competitors make the race fast;
competitors keep the race slow and tactical.

Suppose there is too little relevant information to assign reasonable probabilities to these two race states.
The athlete therefore faces a decision under uncertainty.
A consequence table can still be constructed.
What is missing is the probability distribution over the states.

Cricket example
Suppose the captain again chooses between a fast bowler and a spinner.
The two possible batting responses are:

(S_1): aggressive batting
(S_2): strike rotation

Suppose recent match analysis gives:

(P(S_1) = 0.65)
(P(S_2) = 0.35)

Estimated runs conceded are:



Bowling decision
Aggressive batting
Strike rotation




Fast bowler
11
7


Spin bowler

Now the decision is under risk because probabilities are available for the possible states.
This does not mean the future is known.
The batter may still respond in either way.
The difference is that the captain now has quantitative information about how likely each response is.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Under certainty
The coach knows which reception state will occur.
Only that state needs to be considered.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Under uncertainty
The coach knows the opponent may receive either well or poorly, but has no useful probability information.
The states are known.
Their probabilities are not.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Under risk
Suppose the analyst estimates:

(P() = 0.70)
(P() = 0.30)

The problem is now under risk because probabilities are available.

The alternatives and possible consequences may remain exactly the same. What changes is the information available about the states of nature.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
Week 02: Decision-Making Environments

7.2 Alternatives
What actions can be chosen?
We may denote them by:
[ A_1, A_2, , A_m ]

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
7.3 States of nature
What uncertain future conditions may occur?
We may denote them by:
[ S_1, S_2, , S_n ]

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
7.4 Consequences
What result follows from each action-state combination?
We may denote the consequence by:
[ C_{ij} ]
where (C_{ij}) is the consequence of choosing action (A_i) when state (S_j) occurs.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
7.5 Available information
What do we know about the states?
This final question determines the decision-making environment.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Step 1: Identify the decision maker
The relay coach.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Step 2: Identify the alternatives

(A_1): select Athlete A
(A_2): select Athlete B

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
section: Step 3: Identify the states of nature
text:
Step 3: Identify the states of nature

(S_1): fast opening pace
(S_2): moderate opening pace

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Step 4: Identify the consequence
The consequence is expected 400 m split time.
Smaller values are preferred.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Step 5: Identify the information environment
If the coach knows the opening pace in advance, the decision is under certainty.
If both race states are possible but no reliable probabilities are available, the decision is under uncertainty.
If the analyst estimates:

(P(S_1) = 0.55)
(P(S_2) = 0.45)

then the decision is under risk.
The decision table itself has not changed.
Only the information available has changed.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
6-minute activity: Classify the environment
For each scenario, identify:

the decision maker;
the alternatives;
the state or states of nature;
the consequence;
whether the problem is under certainty, uncertainty, or risk.


Scenario A: Cricket
A captain must choose between spin and pace.
The pitch inspection confirms that the surface will strongly assist spin throughout the next session.
Estimated runs conceded are available for both bowling choices under that known condition.


Scenario B: Athletics
A 1500 m runner must choose between an aggressive and conservative pacing strategy.
The race may become fast or tactical, but the athlete has no reliable estimate of the probability of either race pattern.


Scenario C: Volleyball
A coach chooses between a standard serve and a jump serve.
Video analysis estimates:

(P() = 0.62)
(P() = 0.38)

The probability of winning the rally is estimated for each serve-reception combination.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
text:
Suggested answers

Scenario A
Environment: Certainty
The relevant future condition is treated as known.


Scenario B
Environment: Uncertainty
Several states are possible, but no probabilities are available.


Scenario C
Environment: Risk
Several states are possible and probabilities are available.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
section: Mistake 1: Calling every unknown future event “risk”
text:
Mistake 1: Calling every unknown future event “risk”
In decision theory, uncertainty and risk are not the same.
The distinction depends on whether probabilities can be assigned.

title: Week 02: Decision-Making Environments
section: Mistake 2: Confusing a state of nature with an alternative
text:
Mistake 2: Confusing a state of nature with an alternative
For example:

The opponent receives poorly.

This is not the coach’s action.
It is a possible state of nature.

title: Statistical Decision Theory
text:
Year 3 · Semester 1 · Optional course


A practical introduction to making rational decisions when outcomes are uncertain. We move from payoff and loss tables to decisions under uncertainty and risk, Bayesian updating, decision trees, the value of information, and utility-based choice.

Explore weekly lessons View course structure

title: Statistical Decision Theory
text:
Course overview

COURSE OVERVIEW


From uncertainty to defensible decisions
The course is built around a simple question: when several actions are available and the future is not fully known, how should we choose?
Students first learn to formulate the decision problem clearly. Only then do we introduce a decision rule and interpret what that rule means in context.



What we will study

Decision alternatives, states of nature, consequences, payoff and loss tables
Decision making under certainty, uncertainty, and risk
Maximax, Maximin, Minimax Regret, Hurwicz, and Laplace criteria
Expected Monetary Value, Expected Opportunity Loss, and EVPI
Bayesian updating, posterior decisions, and value of sample information
Decision trees and rollback analysis for sequential decisions
Utility, certainty equivalents, and risk attitudes




Prerequisites
Probability and Distribution Theory I & II, and Inferential Statistics.


Learning approach. Each week starts with a decision problem. We identify the actions, uncertain events, and consequences before introducing the mathematical rule used to choose among the actions.

title: Statistical Decision Theory
text:
Intended learning outcomes

INTENDED LEARNING OUTCOMES


What you should be able to do



1

Formulate statistical decision problems by identifying alternatives, states of nature, consequences, and available information.



2

Apply and interpret decision criteria under uncertainty and risk, including expected value, opportunity loss, and value of information.



3

Use Bayes’ theorem, posterior probabilities, Bayes decision rules, and decision trees for sequential decision problems.



4

Evaluate decisions under risk using utility functions and explain how risk attitudes can alter an optimal decision.

title: Statistical Decision Theory
text:
Weekly lessons

15-WEEK LEARNING PATH

One focused lecture each week, supported by independent problem solving and reading.


Week 01

Introduction to Statistical Decision Theory
Decision problems, alternatives, states of nature, consequences, payoff/loss tables, and the decision-theory process.



Week 02

Decision-Making Environments
Certainty, uncertainty, risk, and formulation of statistical decision problems.



Week 03

Decision under Uncertainty I
Maximax and Maximin criteria for payoff and cost tables.



Week 04

Decision under Uncertainty II
Minimax Regret, Hurwicz, and Laplace criteria.



Week 05

Decision under Risk I
Expected Monetary Value and optimal action under known probabilities.



Week 06

Decision under Risk II
Expected Opportunity Loss and Expected Value of Perfect Information.



Week 07

Extensions of Expected-Value Decisions
Maximum likelihood, continuous outcomes, salvage values, and applications.



Week 08

Prior Information and Bayesian Updating
Priors, likelihoods, Bayes’ theorem, and posterior probabilities.



Week 09

Bayes Decision Rule & Sample Information
Prior and posterior decisions, value and cost of sample information.



Week 10

Bayesian Decision Analysis
Posterior expected payoff/loss and the practical value of additional information.



Week 11

Decision Trees I
Decision nodes, chance nodes, branches, outcomes, probabilities, costs, and payoffs.



Week 12

Decision Trees II
Rollback analysis, expected values, optimal choices, and sequential decisions.



Week 13

Decision Trees III
Sample information, revised probabilities, and multi-stage decisions.



Week 14

Utility Theory I
Utility of money, certainty equivalent, expected utility, and limits of EMV.



Week 15

Utility Theory II & Integrated Analysis
Risk attitudes, utility-based decisions, and synthesis of decision criteria.
